questions.prompt: What is the unit of measurement used to express the refractive power of a lens?
questions.modelAnswer: Diopters.

questions.prompt: In an eye with myopia (nearsightedness), where is the image focused relative to the retina?
questions.modelAnswer: In front of the retina.

questions.prompt: Which type of lens is required to correct hyperopia (farsightedness)?
questions.modelAnswer: Convex lens.

questions.prompt: Define "presbyopia" and identify its primary physiological cause.
questions.modelAnswer: Presbyopia is the loss of the eye's ability to accommodate for near vision due to a stiffening of the lens and loss of elasticity associated with aging.

questions.prompt: What is the underlying cause of astigmatism?
questions.modelAnswer: An irregular or uneven curvature of the cornea or lens.

questions.prompt: Explain why the optic disc is referred to as the "blind spot."
questions.modelAnswer: It is the site of the optic disc, where the optic nerve exits the eye and there are no photoreceptors.

questions.prompt: Which layer of the retina is responsible for absorbing stray light to prevent reflection and for the phagocytosis of photoreceptor discs?
questions.modelAnswer: The pigment epithelium.

questions.prompt: Which form of vitamin A is the light-sensitive component of rhodopsin?
questions.modelAnswer: 11-cis retinal.

questions.prompt: Contrast rods and cones in terms of their sensitivity to light and their role in night vs. day vision.
questions.modelAnswer: Rods have a lower threshold, are highly sensitive to low-intensity light, and mediate night vision. Cones have a higher threshold and mediate day/color vision.

questions.prompt: Which area of the retina contains only cones and provides the highest visual acuity?
questions.modelAnswer: The fovea centralis (within the macula).

questions.prompt: Describe the "dark current" in photoreceptors in terms of ion flow and the second messenger involved.
questions.modelAnswer: The dark current is an inward Na^+ flow through channels held open by high levels of cGMP.

questions.prompt: What specific chemical transformation occurs to retinal immediately upon the absorption of a photon?
questions.modelAnswer: Photoisomerization of 11-cis retinal to all-trans retinal.

questions.prompt: Name the G protein that is activated by metarhodopsin II during the visual cascade.
questions.modelAnswer: Transducin (G_t).

questions.prompt: How does the intracellular concentration of cyclic GMP (cGMP) change when a photoreceptor is exposed to light?
questions.modelAnswer: It decreases (due to activation of phosphodiesterase).

questions.prompt: Does a photoreceptor depolarize or hyperpolarize in response to light?
questions.modelAnswer: It hyperpolarizes.

questions.prompt: What effect does light-induced hyperpolarization of a rod have on the release of the neurotransmitter glutamate?
questions.modelAnswer: It decreases the release of glutamate.

questions.prompt: Which retinal cells are the only ones capable of producing true action potentials?
questions.modelAnswer: Retinal ganglion cells.

questions.prompt: What is the physiological function of horizontal cells in the retina?
questions.modelAnswer: They provide lateral inhibition, which sharpens visual contrast and helps define the boundaries of images.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between an "on-center" and an "off-center" ganglion cell receptive field.
questions.modelAnswer: On-center: Light in the center excites the cell; light in the surround inhibits it. Off-center: Light in the center inhibits the cell; light in the surround excites it.

questions.prompt: Which cranial nerve carries visual information from the eye to the brain?
questions.modelAnswer: Optic nerve (Cranial Nerve II).

questions.prompt: At which anatomical structure do the fibers from the nasal hemiretinas cross the midline?
questions.modelAnswer: The optic chiasm.

questions.prompt: Name the primary thalamic relay nucleus for the visual system.
questions.modelAnswer: The lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN).

questions.prompt: What visual field deficit results from a complete lesion of the optic chiasm?
questions.modelAnswer: Bitemporal heteronymous hemianopia (loss of both temporal visual fields).

questions.prompt: A lesion of the right optic tract will result in what specific type of vision loss?
questions.modelAnswer: Left homonymous hemianopia (loss of the left visual field in both eyes).

questions.prompt: Define "homonymous contralateral hemianopia with macular sparing" and identify the likely site of the lesion.
questions.modelAnswer: It is the loss of the same half of the visual field in both eyes but with central vision intact; it is caused by a lesion of the geniculocalcarine tract (optic radiations) or visual cortex.

questions.prompt: Where in the brain is the primary visual cortex (Brodmann's area 17) located?
questions.modelAnswer: The occipital lobe (banks of the calcarine fissure).

questions.prompt: Which type of visual cortex cell responds best to a stationary bar of light with a specific orientation?
questions.modelAnswer: Simple cells.

questions.prompt: How do "complex cells" in the visual cortex differ from "simple cells" in their stimulus requirements?
questions.modelAnswer: Complex cells respond best to moving bars or edges of light with a specific orientation, whereas simple cells prefer stationary ones.

questions.prompt: What is the mechanism of action of the drug pilocarpine in the treatment of glaucoma?
questions.modelAnswer: It is a cholinergic muscarinic agonist that causes miosis (pupillary constriction), which helps open the canals of Schlemm and improve drainage.

questions.prompt: What is the primary cause of the increased intraocular pressure seen in open-angle glaucoma?
questions.modelAnswer: Increased hydraulic resistance to the outflow of aqueous humor through the trabecular meshwork.
